content:
# Review: grab-bridge reverse-proxy hardening plan

The plan covers CSP-response-stripping, redirect rewriting, and cookie munging. It does **not** cover the following concrete failure cases. Ranked by likelihood on real popular websites.

---

1. **Upstream CSRF check rejects the proxied request because `Origin`/`Referer`/`Sec-Fetch-*` are forwarded as `127.0.0.1`.**
   - **Trigger shape:** Any SaaS dashboard that gates state changes on `Origin` (Stripe dashboard, GitHub, Linear, Vercel, banking sites). The browser sends `Origin: http://127.0.0.1:<port>` and `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`; `copyProxyResponseHeaders`'s request-side sibling passes them through verbatim. Upstream sees an unexpected origin and returns 403/422 or invalidates the session.
   - **User sees:** "Save", "Comment", "Create issue" buttons silently fail with a generic error, or the page kicks back to a login screen.
   - **One-line fix:** In `proxyGrabRequest`, rewrite `origin`, `referer`, and drop `sec-fetch-site`/`sec-fetch-mode`/`sec-fetch-dest` to the proxyTarget's origin before `fetch`.

2. **Service Workers registered by the proxied page install scoped to `127.0.0.1:<port>` and hijack later loads.**
   - **Trigger shape:** Twitter/X, YouTube, Spotify, Instagram, Pinterest — page calls `navigator.serviceWorker.register("/sw.js")`. The bridge proxies `/sw.js` from upstream; the SW installs against the local origin. On the next reload the SW's fetch handler returns upstream-URL responses (or offline fallbacks) for routes that no longer match the bridge.
   - **User sees:** blank page or stale "You're offline" on reload, even though the upstream is fine; caching the broken SW makes it stick.
   - **One-line fix:** Inject an override before the body script that no-ops `navigator.serviceWorker.register`, and serve `/sw.js` (and known SW paths) as 404 from the bridge.

3. **WebSocket / upgrade requests are not proxied (fetch cannot upgrade).**
   - **Trigger shape:** Linear live updates, Notion collab, Slack, GitHub notifications-over-WS — page opens `wss://<upstream>/socket` (or builds the URL from `window.location.host`, becoming `ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/socket`). The bridge's `http.createServer` has no `'upgrade'` handler; the socket is dropped, and if the URL was absolute to the upstream origin, the browser sends it with cookies scoped to `127.0.0.1` so the upstream WS handshake 401s.
   - **User sees:** page loads but never receives realtime updates; collaborative cursors/comments never appear.
   - **One-line fix:** Add an `'upgrade'` listener on the bridge server that tunnels raw bytes to a TLS socket connected to `proxyTarget` (host/port preserved), and rewrite the WS URL's `Host` header.

4. **`<base href="https://upstream.example.com/">` in the HTML makes every relative URL resolve against the upstream origin.**
   - **Trigger shape:** Shopify storefronts, Blogger/Blogspot, many WordPress themes, some marketing pages. The base tag survives the response (the plan only rewrites the `Location` header, not the body). After the base tag, `/assets/app.js`, `/login`, `./next` all resolve to `https://upstream.example.com/...` and escape the bridge.
   - **User sees:** CSS/JS 404 (broken styling) or first click navigates away from `127.0.0.1` and the overlay disappears.
   - **One-line fix:** In the HTML-injection step, strip or rewrite `<base href="...">` to point at the bridge origin before inserting the overlay script.

5. **`<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="...">` survives because only the response header is stripped.**
   - **Trigger shape:** Sites that declare CSP via meta (Notion public pages, Google properties, WordPress plugins, many legacy CMS pages). The plan strips the `Content-Security-Policy` response header but the meta tag is still in the body and is honored by the browser — `script-src 'self'` etc. silently kills the `raven-grab.js` script if its effective policy excludes the bridge origin, or blocks the inline config if `'unsafe-inline'` is missing.
   - **User sees:** panel never boots, no console error visible to the designer.
   - **One-line fix:** Strip `<meta http-equiv="content-security-policy">` (case-insensitive) from the HTML body in the same injection pass that adds the script.

6. **302 with a scheme mismatch (`http://upstream` vs `https://upstream`) is treated as offsite and the browser escapes the bridge.**
   - **Trigger shape:** Login flows on some banking and enterprise SaaS sites that issue `Location: http://host/...` after auth, or HTTP→HTTPS upgrade chains where the upstream's own redirect uses a different scheme than `proxyTarget`. The plan's "origin equals proxyTarget's origin" comparison is scheme-sensitive, so `http://upstream` ≠ `https://upstream` → left alone with `x-raven-proxy-offsite`.
   - **User sees:** login completes but the browser is now on the real upstream origin; overlay is gone and the session is lost.
   - **One-line fix:** Compare origins on hostname+port only (ignore scheme) when deciding whether to rewrite `Location`.

7. **`Permissions-Policy` (and legacy `Feature-Policy`) header is not in the stripped set and disables features the overlay uses.**
   - **Trigger shape:** Sites that send `Permissions-Policy: clipboard=(), camera=(), geolocation=()` (Notion, Google Docs, Figma embeds, some news sites). The plan strips COEP/COOP/CORP but not `permissions-policy`. The overlay's "copy snippet to clipboard" or screenshot feature is silently disabled by the browser.
   - **User sees:** "Copy" button in the Raven panel does nothing; no visible error in the panel.
   - **One-line fix:** Add `permissions-policy` and `feature-policy` to the stripped response-headers set.

8. **`<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0; url=https://upstream/...">` in the HTML navigates the browser away from the bridge.**
   - **Trigger shape:** Legacy SSO / interstitial pages, some old login redirects, marketing redirectors. The plan rewrites `Location` headers but not meta-refresh in the body; the browser performs a top-level navigation to the upstream origin before the overlay has time to bind.
   - **User sees:** the proxied page flashes then jumps to the real upstream URL, overlay never appears.
   - **One-line fix:** Rewrite the URL in meta-refresh tags (or strip the tag) during the HTML injection pass.

9. **Non-UTF-8 HTML is corrupted by `Buffer.toString("utf8")` + `Buffer.from(html, "utf8")`.**
   - **Trigger shape:** International popular sites: Baidu, Weibo, Yandex, regional government portals — `Content-Type: text/html; charset=gb2312` (or `<meta charset=gb2312>`). The code decodes the body as UTF-8, re-encodes as UTF-8, but leaves the original `Content-Type: charset=gb2312` header intact, so the browser reinterprets the UTF-8 bytes as gb2312 → mojibake. Also, `Content-Length` is recomputed (good) but the charset mismatch is not.
   - **User sees:** garbled text on the proxied page; overlay text may also be corrupted; designer thinks the site itself is broken.
   - **One-line fix:** Detect charset from the `Content-Type`/`<meta charset>`, decode accordingly, and either re-encode in the original charset or rewrite the `<meta charset>` and `Content-Type` to `utf-8` after transcoding.

10. **`Alt-Svc` response header survives and poisons subsequent loads to `127.0.0.1:443`.**
    - **Trigger shape:** Cloudflare/HTTP/2-fronted sites that emit `Alt-Svc: h2=":443"`. The header is not stripped; the browser caches the alt-svc mapping for `127.0.0.1:<port>` and on the next request attempts h2 to `127.0.0.1:443` (which is not the bridge) → connection fails until the alt-svc entry expires.
    - **User sees:** first load works, subsequent loads intermittently hang or fail with `ERR_CONNECTION_CLOSED` until the browser flushes alt-svc cache.
    - **One-line fix:** Add `alt-svc` to the stripped response-headers set.

---

### Notes on plan correctness (not failures, but gaps the brief should call out)

- The plan says "pass the same config object through the same-origin script URL instead" but does not explicitly state that the proxy path must **stop calling `grabConfigTag()`**. If the implementer keeps the inline `grabConfigTag` output AND adds the `cfg=` script, the inline tag is still blocked by any meta-CSP (see #5) and the panel boots only because of the URL form — the inline dead code is harmless but the brief is ambiguous about removing it.
- The `Sec-Fetch-*` family is the same root cause as #1 and is browser-set (not strippable from the request side via `strippedRequestHeaders` because the browser will re-add them) — but the bridge can strip them in its outbound `fetch` `headers` object since they're copied from `req.rawHeaders`. Worth being explicit.
- The plan's cookie rewrite handles `Set-Cookie` on the response but never rewrites `Cookie` on the **request** side; if upstream sets a cookie with `Path=/app` and the browser later sends it back to `127.0.0.1:port/app`, that is fine — but if upstream also expects a `Host`-bound cookie that the browser will NOT send to `127.0.0.1` at all (cookies the browser has stored for the upstream origin and would normally send to upstream), those are simply absent from the proxied request. This is an inherent limitation of same-origin proxying and the plan should state it explicitly so operators don't expect "logged in via existing browser session" to carry over.
